results.title: What an H100 hour lists for at Azure and Oracle, next to the rental marketplaces (with the VM named) - Show and Tell - Hugging Face Forums
highlights:
“From $X per GPU-hour” is the number everyone quotes for the big clouds, usually without saying which machine you have to rent to get it. I added two clouds whose price lists can be read without an account — Azure and Oracle Cloud — to the rental prices we already collect hourly, and kept the machine attached to every number.

One reading, 2 Oct 2026, 13:00 UTC, USD per GPU-hour:

| GPU | Vast.ai median (offers) | RunPod from | Azure from | Oracle Cloud from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 | 0.74 (58) | 1.39 | 3.40 — ND96asr v4, 8 × 40 GB, VM 27.20/h | 3.05 — BM.GPU4.8, 8 × 40 GB, machine 24.40/h |
| H100 | 2.27 (8) | 2.69 | 6.98 — NC40ads H100 v5, 1 × 94 GB | 10.00 — BM.GPU.H100.8, 8 × 80 GB, machine 80.00/h |
| H200 | 5.12 (7) | 3.59 | 10.60 — ND96isr H200 v5, 8 × 141 GB, VM 84.80/h | 10.00 — BM.GPU.H200.8, 8 × 141 GB, machine 80.00/h |
| B200 | 7.81 (6) | 5.98 | not listed as its own size | 14.00 — BM.GPU.B200.8, 8 × 180 GB, machine 112.00/h |

Three things the table shows at this reading:

1. The per-GPU price hides the unit of sale. Azure’s H100 at 6.98 is a one-card VM you can take alone. Oracle’s 10.00 exists only as an eight-card bare-metal machine at 80.00 an hour. For the A100 both clouds’ lowest per-GPU price sits in an eight-card machine with the 40 GB card; a single 80 GB A100 on Azure lists at 3.67.
2. The gap to the marketplace is larger on the two older cards. List price against the Vast.ai median of the same hour: A100 4.6× (Azure) and 4.1× (Oracle), H100 3.1× and 4.4×; H200 about 2× for both, B200 1.8× (Oracle). One reading, and the marketplace side is thin for the newer classes (six to eight offers) — a description of today, not a trend.
3. The two clouds do not rank the same way per class. Oracle is below Azure on the A100 and the H200, above it on the H100.

What it does not say: availability (a list price is not free capacity), what you pay with a commitment or a negotiated rate, or that a cloud VM and a marketplace host are the same product — they are not; the table compares prices, nothing else.

How the numbers are made: Azure publishes whole-VM prices per region, so the per-GPU price is the Linux pay-as-you-go price divided by the GPU count from Microsoft’s size documentation, lowest across documented sizes and public regions; sizes the price list carries but the documentation does not describe are left out rather than guessed. Oracle prices a GPU-hour directly and has one list without regions. Both are read four times a day and shown beside the marketplace medians, never blended into them.

results.title: If AI Model Prices Fall, Can Oracle's Cloud Contracts Reprice Fast Enough? - AI Tech Model
results.author: Steve Levine
highlights:
No, Oracle's cloud contracts cannot reprice fast enough when AI model prices fall. They lock in physical GPU capacity at fixed hourly rates, while model inference gets cheaper on a separate track. Universal Credits is Oracle's prepaid model for buying cloud use in advance. According to Oracle's Universal Credits FAQ, buyers make a minimum 12-month prepaid commitment drawn down by metered use, with unused credits expiring and nonrefundable.

...

## What is Oracle actually selling?

Oracle reported fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $19.3B with more than $30B in new AI cloud contracts. Remaining performance obligations reached $664B, up $209B year over year, according to Oracle's September 2026 results announcement.

Oracle said it delivered more than 300,000 GPUs to AI cloud customers since fiscal Q4 2026 and added 850MW of datacenter capacity. Those contracts reserve physical compute, not per-token model prices. Oracle publishes fixed hourly infrastructure rates such as $10 per GPU-hour for H100 and H200 and $3.05 for A100, applied uniformly across regions.

...

Customers on fixed GPU-capacity commitments cannot capture model-price deflation until renewal. Prepaid credits do not roll over when models get cheaper. Fixed GPU-hour rates keep applying even when a newer model cuts tokens per task.

results.title: Tencent scores 100000 offshore AI chip deal with Oracle for $7 billion ...
results.author: Shane Downing
highlights:
Oracle has reportedly made a deal with Tencent for a five-year lease at several Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia, covering about 100,000 advanced AI chips unavailable in China. The deal is estimated to be worth about $7 billion, which would come out to about $1.60 per chip per hour over five years, with about 30% upfront, according to a report by the Financial Times (FT). The deal lands as compute rental prices continue to climb, per Chief Strategy Officer James Mitchell on Tencent’s August 12 earnings call. Neither company has commented on the report, but such leases are legal under current U.S. rules, per the FT.

The estimated chip-hour price is around 43% less than the roughly $2.80 per GPU-hour for Nvidia’s H100 with a one-year contract, per research firm SemiAnalysis in August. It’s also about 48% lower than the $3.09 per GPU-hour for a three-year contract with Nvidia’s B200, per a 2025 filing by Japanese data center operator Datasection for an unnamed customer. Market trends have pricing running the other way, with the FT reporting longer terms and larger upfront payments for such leases. Tencent president Martin Lau said on the same call the company could sell its existing orders at “more than 30% profit” compared to what it “paid just a few months ago.”

No chips are named. The FT says that such leases could reach even Nvidia’s top processors, but that does not mean this deal involves Nvidia hardware. One-year H100 contracts on SemiAnalysis’s index were above the estimated rate at about $1.70 per GPU-hour even as of October 2025, with the B200 rate being even more expensive despite its longer, three-year term. Going by raw B200 server costs, which exclude buildings, power, networking, and financing, 100,000 B200s would cost $5.44 billion, or about 78% of the reported value, based on Datasection’s 2025 purchase of servers with 5,000 B200s for $272 million.

...

The reported deal comes weeks before Oracle’s Investor Day on Oct. 28 in Las Vegas, during its Oct. 25–28 Oracle AI World event at the Venetian. That would be a chance for the company to disclose details about the deal, such as announcing what hardware is to be leased. Given the hardware math, our assumption is that it involves older or non-Nvidia hardware rather than an action born of financial stress at Oracle. The month following Oracle’s event, Tencent is expected to report its Q3 results. These events could also reveal more concrete details about the arrangement.

results.title: GPU Prices 2026: H100 From $3.49/hr, RTX 5070 at +58%
results.author: Axis Intelligence Research
highlights:
> Prices verified on October 2, 2026. Every price on this page was read from the vendor’s live pricing page, public price API or retail listing on that date. AWS Capacity Block rates effective October 7, 2026 are taken from AWS’s own announcement on its pricing page.

...

In the cloud, an NVIDIA H100 lists between $3.49 and $12.29 per GPU-hour on-demand; the neocloud median is $3.99. A B200 lists from $6.69 to $8.60. On the consumer side, the cheapest new RTX 5070 on Newegg was $869.99 against a $549 launch price — 58% above MSRP.

...

1. According to Axis Intelligence Research, hyperscalers list the NVIDIA H100 at 2.93 times the neocloud median price — $11.68 versus $3.99 per GPU-hour on-demand, as of October 2, 2026 (GPU Hour Premium Ratio, GHPR).
2. AWS raises EC2 Capacity Block GPU rates about 15% effective October 7, 2026, taking an H100 accelerator-hour from $5.191 to $5.970 and a B200 from $12.355 to $14.208, per AWS’s pricing page.
3. An 8-GPU H100 server rented on-demand for three years costs $2.58 million on Azure and $734,000 on Runpod, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s list-price TCO calculation.
4. The cheapest new GeForce RTX 5070 on Newegg cost $869.99 on October 2, 2026, 58% above the $549 price NVIDIA announced at CES in January 2025.
5. Azure’s spot price for an 8x H100 VM is 82% below its own on-demand rate — $18.17 versus $98.32 per hour in US East, per Microsoft’s Retail Prices API.

...

### H100 on-demand price per GPU-hour by provider (October 2, 2026)

| Provider | Instance / SKU | Listed price | GPUs | Price per GPU-hour | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Runpod | H100 SXM Pod (Secure Cloud) | $3.49/hr | 1 | $3.49 | Runpod pricing |
| Lambda | NVIDIA H100 SXM instance | $3.99/GPU/hr | 1–8 | $3.99 | Lambda pricing |
| CoreWeave | NVIDIA HGX H100 (North America) | $49.24/hr | 8 | $6.16 | CoreWeave pricing |
| Google Cloud | a3-highgpu-8g, us-central1 | $88.49/hr | 8 | $11.06 | Google Cloud accelerator-optimized pricing |
| Microsoft Azure | ND96isr H100 v5, East US | $98.32/hr | 8 | $12.29 | Azure Retail Prices API |

...

AWS’s per-accelerator figure that we verified is the EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML rate — a reservation you book for a fixed window, not open-ended on-demand. On October 2, 2026 the p5.48xlarge (8x H100) Capacity Block rate in US East (N. Virginia) was $41.528 per instance-hour, or $5.191 per H100. AWS’s pricing page states that from October 7, 2026, the P5 rate becomes $5.970 per accelerator across all available regions. Axis Intelligence Research did not verify a current AWS on-demand p5 rate for this snapshot, so AWS is excluded from the on-demand table rather than estimated.

## Why Is AWS Raising GPU Prices in October 2026?

AWS publishes the reason in one line: Capacity Block reservation prices are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand. The October 7, 2026 update moves every GPU family up by the same proportion.

### AWS EC2 Capacity Block rate change, effective October 7, 2026

| Instance family | GPU | Rate before (per accelerator-hour) | Rate from Oct 7, 2026 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | B300 | $14.040 | $16.146 | +15.0% |
| P6-B200 | B200 | $12.355 | $14.208 | +15.0% |
| P5en | H200 | $6.865 | $7.895 | +15.0% |
| P5e | H200 | $5.970 | $6.866 | +15.0% |
| P5 | H100 | $5.191 | $5.970 | +15.0% |
| P4de | A100 80GB | $2.214 | $2.546 | +15.0% |
| P4d | A100 40GB | $1.475 | $1.696 | +15.0% |

Source: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing, retrieved October 2, 2026. “Before” rates are the US East (N. Virginia) or US-region rates listed on the same page; percentage change is an Axis Intelligence Research calculation.

...

## How Much Does a B200 or H200 Cost per Hour?

### Blackwell and H200 per-GPU-hour prices (October 2, 2026)

| GPU | Provider | Pricing model | Price per GPU-hour | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | Lambda | On-demand instance | $6.69 | Lambda pricing |
| B200 | Runpod | On-demand Pod | $6.79 | Runpod pricing |
| B200 | CoreWeave | On-demand, 8x HGX ($68.80/hr) | $8.60 | CoreWeave pricing |
| B200 | Lambda | 1-Click Cluster, 256+ GPUs, 2 weeks–1 year | $8.87 | Lambda pricing |
| B200 | Google Cloud | DWS Flex-start, a4-highgpu-8g ($64.44/hr) | $8.06 | Google Cloud pricing |
| B200 | AWS | Capacity Block, from Oct 7, 2026 | $14.21 | AWS pricing |
| B300 | Runpod | On-demand Pod | $7.89 | Runpod pricing |
| H200 | Runpod | On-demand Pod | $4.59 | Runpod pricing |

| H200 | Google Cloud | On-demand, a3-ultragpu-8g ($84.81/hr) | $10.60 | Google Cloud pricing |

One detail that most rate cards hide: Lambda’s B200 is cheaper on-demand ($6.69) than in its own 1-Click Clusters ($8.87–$9.86). The cluster price buys guaranteed multi-node capacity with interconnect, not a per-GPU discount. Google Cloud does not list an on-demand price for its A4 (B200) VM at all; the cheapest public path is DWS Flex-start at $64.44 per 8-GPU hour.

results.title: Nebius did exactly what it said it would. Last week's Pulse flagged the on-demand increases Nebius had posted for October 1. Our October 4 catalog capture yesterday shows them in place, in … | Bobby Clay
results.author: Bobby Clay
highlights:
# Nebius did exactly what it said it would. Last week's Pulse flagged the on-demand increases Nebius had posted for October 1. Our October 4 catalog capture yesterday shows them in place, in … | Bobby Clay · LinkedIn · 2026-10-05T00:00:00+00:00

**Bobby Clay**.

---

Nebius did exactly what it said it would. Last week's Pulse flagged the on-demand increases Nebius had posted for October 1. Our October 4 catalog capture yesterday shows them in place, in dollars per GPU-hour:

H100: $3.85 to $4.50
H200: $4.50 to $5.40
B200: $7.15 to $8.50
B300: $7.85 to $9.50

That changed the lowest observed H100 list price across the nine providers we track. On September 27 it was Nebius at $3.85 per GPU-hour. On October 4 it was Crusoe at $3.90.
Everything else held. Of 14,001 GPU price listings in the October 4 catalog, 13,996 matched a September 27 listing, and the 20 Nebius listings were the only verified changes above 1%.

The transaction side moved on its own path. OCPI for H200 went from $4.84 on September 28 to $5.57 on October 4. Over the same stretch, the lowest H200 list price we track held at $4.29 (Crusoe). List prices and transaction prices measure different things, and this week the gap between them widened. If you buy on-demand capacity from a Neocloud, posted price notices are worth tracking. This one landed on schedule, to the cent.

The full issue, with every provider's lowest observed price and the method notes, is here:
https://lnkd.in/efqfwQWm

These are public catalog list prices, not live quotes, and a listing does not establish capacity or orderability.

results.title: Nebius just confirmed the price increase we flagged as unconfirmed last week. Its live now. | Devanshu Rajput
results.author: Devanshu Rajput
highlights:
Nebius just confirmed the price increase we flagged as unconfirmed last week. Its live now.

H100 pricing on Nebius went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour, confirmed directly against their own pricing page, a 17% increase. H200 rose 20%, from $4.50 to $5.40. B300 climbed 21%, reaching $9.50. This is Nebius's second rate hike since May, when H100 was still priced at $2.95.

According to GetDeploying's pricing tracker, the median on-demand H100 across 40 providers sat at $3.42/GPU-hour as of September 28, up 15% year over year. The same tracker puts hyperscaler pricing at roughly 58% above specialized GPU clouds for the same chip.

results.title: Nebius and CoreWeave Lift Nvidia GPU Prices by Up to 21% - Daily Market Chronicle
highlights:
Nvidia rental prices are rising even for last-generation H100s. Nebius has posted an October 1, 2026 on-demand card that lifts selected Nvidia GPU-hour rates by 16.9% to 21.0%. CoreWeave said on September 17 that it is still signing compute at higher prices, including short contracts at about $40 million per megawatt of annualized revenue. A landlord can charge more for a chip it does not make only while that chip stays scarce. That is the signal behind Nvidia, and it is the opposite of a capacity glut.

Nebius’s price page, checked on October 2, still prints two columns. On-demand H100 is $3.85 per GPU-hour. The column marked effective October 1 is $4.50. The same split runs through the H200, the B200, and the B300. Reuters reported on September 17 that this was the second pay-as-you-go increase in about three months, with selected Nvidia GPU rates up 17% to 21%. The card on nebius.com/prices matches that range. It does not show every customer already paying the new rate.

## The card Nebius posted

Four Nvidia rows have a public before and after. GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 racks are still “contact us” in both columns. RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80. L40S “from” rates do not move. The hike lands on the accelerators customers are queued for.

| Nvidia GPU | Prior on-demand column | Announced October 1 card | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HGX H100 | $3.85 | $4.50 | +$0.65, or 16.9% |
| HGX H200 | $4.50 | $5.40 | +$0.90, or 20.0% |
| HGX B200 | $7.15 | $8.50 | +$1.35, or 18.9% |
| HGX B300 | $7.85 | $9.50 | +$1.65, or 21.0% |

...

Announced Nebius on-demand rates for October 1, 2026, set against the prior on-demand column still printed on the same page. These are posted card rates, not a receipt. The live page and a third-party tracker still disagree, so this chart does not show what every customer is paying. Source: nebius.com/prices, checked October 2, 2026.

...

October 2 is after the effective date, and the page still shows both numbers. The left-hand label is still “On-demand, GPU-hour.” The right-hand label is “GPU-hour (Effective October 1, 2026).” A customer cannot tell, from the page alone, which figure the console will bill.

GPU Finder’s Nebius page, with availability checked at 06:23 UTC on October 2, still listed one-GPU on-demand rates of $3.85 for the H100, $7.15 for the B200, and $7.85 for the B300. Those are the old column. The same check already showed the H200 at $5.40, the new column, with a spot print of $2.45 beside it. The H100 spot print on that row was $2.15. The tracker has not frozen. It has moved one of the four headline GPUs and left the other three on the pre-October number. Treating the whole book as repriced at midnight on October 1 would be tidier, and it would be wrong.

results.title: AWS Capacity Blocks: ~15% GPU Hike Oct 7 | explainx.ai Blog | explainx.ai
results.author: Yash Thakker
highlights:
Effective October 7, 2026, Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML charge more for reserved NVIDIA accelerators. AWS published a single new hourly rate per family across all available regions: P6-B300 $16.146 ($16.819 GovCloud), P6-B200 $14.208 ($14.801 GovCloud), P5en $7.895, P5e $6.866, P5 $5.970, P4de $2.546, P4d $1.696. Compared with the tables still on that same page today, those US-listed NVIDIA families move about 15%.

This is a run-cost event, not a market-color event. If you already planned a reserved GPU block for a training run, a fine-tune window, or a burst of H100/H200/B200/B300 capacity, the invoice changes. On-Demand and Savings Plans do not move with this notice. The reservation fee is locked when you buy, even if the block starts after October 7. That is the mechanism. Use it or pay the new list.

...

## The official October 7 rates (cite this page, not a recap)

AWS's announcement on the Capacity Blocks pricing page is the primary source. Quote it as written: reservation prices "are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand."
